title: Claudia Rankine: White supremacy has overrun America
gist: In an interview around her new book Triage, poet Claudia Rankine argues that Trump merely gave America's white supremacy 'an overt leader, not an overt reality' since the underlying reality was always there, and describes increasingly spending time in Marseille as an alternative space given her sense that the problem is entrenched in the US.

insights.claim: Claudia Rankine's Triage, her first book in six years, blends poetry, narrative, memoir, criticism and photography, following two female characters — an unnamed narrator and 'the theorist' — navigating the fissures in their friendship against 'the wreckage of our world today'.
insights.speaker: Franklin Nelson
insights.so_what: Establishes what the new book is and how it departs formally from her prior work.
insights.quote: Published in August, it blends poetry, narrative, memoir, criticism and photography as it presents two female characters—the unnamed narrator and “the theorist”—navigating the fissures in their friendship across time and space, as well as “the wreckage of our world today”.
insights.locator: Triage, Rankine's first book in six years

insights.claim: Rankine says Triage differs from her earlier books Citizen and Just Us because those books needed to document what racial injustice looked like, whereas now — with climate change, war in Ukraine and Gaza, and family separations from deportation — 'there is no failure of documentation in this moment', so the driving question has shifted to what to do about it.
insights.speaker: Claudia Rankine
insights.so_what: Marks a shift in Rankine's project from bearing witness to grappling with agency and response once the facts are already visible to everyone.
insights.quote: We know climate change is here to stay. We know people are being murdered wilfully in Ukraine, Gaza and many places. We know people are being deported, children are being ripped from their parents. There is no failure of documentation in this moment.

insights.claim: Rankine says her central question in the new book is 'what are we going to do?' — how people can avoid simply sitting by while crises unfold, given the limits of liberal politics and personal agency in an atomised, volatile world.
insights.speaker: Claudia Rankine
insights.so_what: Frames the book's core preoccupation as agency and response rather than diagnosis alone.
insights.quote: The question is: what are we going to do? Or even, more simply, what is there to do? How can we just sit by and let it all just go down in this way?

insights.claim: Rankine says her career as a creative writing teacher at New York University gave her the confidence to write Triage in a way she would not have had 30 years earlier, calling herself 'in training for this book'.
insights.speaker: Claudia Rankine
insights.so_what: Ties the formal ambition of the new book to her long teaching career, not just accumulated life experience.
insights.quote: It’s almost as if I have been in training for this book,” she adds. Without her teaching background, “I wouldn’t have had the confidence to write it 30 years ago”.

insights.claim: Rankine says every book she has written has been about the entrenchment of white supremacy in America, and argues that Donald Trump gave white supremacy 'an overt leader, not an overt reality' — the underlying reality, she says, was always there.
insights.speaker: Claudia Rankine
insights.so_what: States Rankine's central political claim that names the article: Trump is a symptom of pre-existing white supremacy, not its cause.
insights.quote: Every book I’ve written has been about the takeover of white supremacy. It wasn’t like it was a secret. ... The only thing that [Donald] Trump has done is give white supremacy an overt leader, not an overt reality. The reality was always there.

insights.claim: Triage grew out of exchanges with scholars and friends including Judith Butler, Sarah Schulman and Homi K Bhabha, and Rankine describes it as a 'performance of the difficult conversations we've been having'.
insights.speaker: Franklin Nelson
insights.so_what: Situates the book's intellectual origins within a specific circle of contemporary theorists and writers.
insights.quote: Born of exchanges with scholars and friends such as Judith Butler, Sarah Schulman and Homi K Bhabha, Rankine describes her eighth book as a “product of now” and a “performance of the difficult conversations we’ve been having”.

insights.claim: Given what she views as the entrenchment of white supremacy in the US, Rankine plans to spend more time in Marseille, home to the Racial Imaginary Institute, a multidisciplinary platform examining race that she co-founded in 2016.
insights.speaker: Franklin Nelson
insights.so_what: Shows a concrete personal response to her political diagnosis: relocating time and institutional focus abroad.

insights.claim: Rankine describes Marseille as one of the few places in Europe where, as a person of colour, she can walk down the street without being 'the news', calling it 'very alive' and a place where 'things are still possible'.
insights.speaker: Claudia Rankine
insights.so_what: Explains the specific personal and racial-safety appeal of Marseille as an alternative base to the US.
insights.quote: It’s one of the few places in Europe where you walk down the street [as a person of colour] and you’re not the news. It’s also very alive. Things are still possible here.
